title: Analysis: EVs are now nine times cheaper than petrol or diesel to drive in the UK  - Carbon Brief
gist: A geopolitics-driven oil shock (oil above $100/bbl, UK diesel up 38% to £1.96/l, petrol up 31% to £1.72/l) has made UK EVs up to nine times cheaper per mile than petrol or diesel cars when charged off-peak (2.3p vs ~20-21p per mile). The cost gap survives the expected January 2027 electricity price-cap rise and a planned 3p/mile EV road tax from April 2028, while battery EVs reached ~30% of UK new-car sales in August.

themes.theme: Oil shock and UK pump prices

insights.claim: UK average diesel prices have risen 38% since February 2026 to £1.96 a litre, and are expected to pass a record £2 a litre following the 20 September attack on Russia's Kapotnya refinery and rising Middle East tensions.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Record diesel prices squeeze UK freight/logistics margins and household budgets; watch for £2/l as a political and demand-destruction threshold.
insights.locator: Following the attack on the Kapotnya oil refinery

insights.claim: Russia, previously the world's second-largest diesel exporter, had its refineries hit on average every three days in the first six months of 2026, tightening global diesel supply.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Sustained attacks on Russian refining support elevated diesel crack spreads and benefit non-Russian refiners with export capacity.
insights.quote: Russia was the second-largest exporter of diesel in the world, but its refineries have been hit every three days on average in the first six months of 2026.
insights.locator: (Russia was the second-largest exporter of diesel

insights.claim: UK petrol prices have risen 31% since February 2026 to an average £1.72 a litre, with some locations nearing £2 per litre.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Petrol inflation feeds directly into UK CPI and consumer discretionary spending pressure.
insights.locator: Similarly, petrol prices have surged by 31%

insights.claim: Oil prices have climbed above $100 per barrel, roughly 50% higher than in June 2026, driven by escalating conflict between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia on top of the US attack on Iran in February.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A Middle East conflict premium of this size is a macro inflation shock; position for energy-sector strength and oil-importer weakness while the conflict escalates.
insights.locator: These increases have been driven by oil prices

insights.claim: In the UK, driving a diesel car now costs about 21p per mile and a petrol car about 20.1p per mile, versus 2.3p per mile for an EV charged on an off-peak tariff, making EVs roughly nine times cheaper to run.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A near order-of-magnitude running-cost gap strengthens the consumer case for EV adoption and home-charging/smart-tariff offerings.
insights.locator: As such, it now costs an estimated 21p per mile

insights.claim: Even when charged at the UK domestic electricity price cap rather than an off-peak tariff, an EV costs about 7p per mile to drive, roughly three times cheaper than petrol or diesel; equivalently, price-cap charging costs about 60p per litre-equivalent versus £1.72 petrol, and off-peak charging about 20p.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The EV cost advantage is robust even without optimised tariffs, so it does not depend on niche smart-charging behaviour.
insights.locator: Even if charging with electricity bought at the domestic price cap

insights.claim: UK drivers can save around £80 per full-tank-equivalent by charging an EV at home instead of filling a petrol car at the pump.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A tangible per-fill saving is a strong marketing hook for EV makers and home-charger installers.

insights.claim: UK EV drivers' annual fuel-cost savings versus petrol drivers have risen from about £1,100 (June 2026 estimate) to about £1,200 a year after the latest fuel price hike.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Rising annual savings improve EV total-cost-of-ownership versus higher upfront prices, supporting used and new EV demand.
insights.locator: Separate analysis from Carbon Brief in June

insights.claim: Public EV charging in the UK remains significantly more expensive than domestic rates, but the government estimates around 90% of EV charging happens at home, limiting the impact on the average running-cost advantage.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: EV economics hinge on home-charging access; drivers without driveways face a narrower gap, a structural constraint for public-charging operators' pricing power and adoption among renters.
insights.locator: Public charging points remain significantly more expensive

themes.theme: Electricity price outlook and gas pass-through

insights.claim: The UK Ofgem price cap rise in October 2026 is almost entirely on gas, with the electricity unit rate expected to rise under 1%, from 26.1p to 26.3p per unit.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Near-term EV charging costs are insulated from the fossil-fuel shock, widening the EV advantage this winter.
insights.locator: The price cap is set to increase in October

insights.claim: A roughly 20% increase in UK price-cap electricity unit rates is expected in January 2027 as higher gas costs filter through to wholesale electricity prices, yet EVs would still remain far cheaper to drive than petrol or diesel cars.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Gas-linked UK power pricing transmits fossil shocks with a lag; a 20% January step-up is a watch item for utilities, household inflation and EV cost comparisons.
insights.locator: A larger 20% increase in electricity unit rates

insights.claim: Petrol cars still make up 55% of the roughly 35 million cars on UK roads, while fully battery-electric vehicles are only 6% and plug-in hybrids a further 3%.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The UK fleet is still overwhelmingly fossil-fuelled, implying a long runway for EV fleet turnover and continued household exposure to oil shocks.
insights.locator: Despite their much higher running costs, petrol still dominates

insights.claim: Battery EVs made up around 30% of new cars sold in the UK in August 2026, up from 26.5% in August 2025, according to the SMMT.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Steady share gains in new sales, likely reinforced by the fuel-price shock, support UK EV sellers and charging infrastructure demand.
insights.locator: However, sales of EVs are continuing to increase

insights.claim: The UK government plans a pay-per-mile tax on EVs from April 2028 that would add 3p per mile, but EVs would still remain far cheaper to drive than petrol or diesel cars given the fuel-cost gap.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Even with 3p/mile tax, off-peak EV running costs (~5.3p) stay far below ~20p for ICE, so the policy is unlikely to derail the EV cost case.
insights.locator: In addition, the government plans to introduce a pay-per-mile tax
